nameStory: Philadelphia fleabane gets its name from the old belief that dried fleabane plants could repel fleas when scattered around homes. The 'Philadelphia' part comes from where botanists first formally described this species. While we now know it doesn't actually chase away fleas, the name stuck from those hopeful colonial days!
description: Philadelphia fleabane is a cheerful wildflower that looks like a small daisy with incredibly thin, thread-like white or pale pink petals radiating from a yellow center. This native perennial typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat fuzzy, branching stem. It's one of our most common spring and early summer wildflowers, often forming loose colonies in open areas where it creates delicate clouds of tiny daisy-like blooms.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Numerous tiny white or pale pink daisy-like flowers with 50-100 extremely narrow, thread-like petals around a bright yellow center - the petals are so thin they look almost hair-like

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are spoon-shaped with rounded tips and often have small teeth, while upper leaves clasp the stem with heart-shaped bases - all leaves feel somewhat soft and fuzzy

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms branching clusters 1-3 feet tall, often growing in loose colonies with multiple flowering stems arising from the base

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels softly hairy or fuzzy to the touch, with a slightly sticky quality on the stems when crushed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces fluffy white seed heads similar to dandelions but much smaller, with seeds that blow away on silky parachutes

habitat: Philadelphia fleabane thrives in moist to moderately dry open areas throughout New England, including meadows, field edges, roadsides, and disturbed soils. It particularly loves spots with some moisture like stream banks, wet meadows, and the edges of marshes. You'll often find it mixed with other common wildflowers like goldenrod and wild asters in sunny to partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin blooming in late spring, with the characteristic fuzzy leaves appearing first in rosettes close to the ground.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late spring through mid-summer, with the tiny daisy-like flowers creating showy displays that attract numerous small pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Blooming continues into early fall, followed by the development of fluffy white seedheads that disperse on autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving only underground roots and possibly some basal leaf rosettes in protected areas.

funFact: Philadelphia fleabane flowers have some of the most numerous petals of any daisy-family plant in New England - each tiny flower head can have 50 to 150 incredibly thin petals, making them look like miniature white fireworks when viewed up close!
confusionNotes: Philadelphia fleabane is easily confused with other fleabanes, especially daisy fleabane, but Philadelphia fleabane has many more petals (50-150 vs. 50 or fewer), and its upper leaves distinctly clasp the stem with heart-shaped bases. Remember: 'Philadelphia has more flair' - meaning more petals and more obvious stem-clasping leaves.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'fleabane' is shared by several different Erigeron species, which can cause confusion when trying to identify them. Philadelphia fleabane is also sometimes called 'common fleabane' or 'poor robin's plantain,' but these names are used for other species too, making the scientific name particularly useful for precise identification.
compareHints: Among New England's fleabanes, Philadelphia fleabane stands out with its extremely numerous thread-like petals (50-150) compared to daisy fleabane's fewer, broader petals (typically under 50). Its stem-clasping upper leaves with heart-shaped bases also distinguish it from robin's plantain, which has more rounded, non-clasping leaves. The tiny individual flowers and soft, fuzzy texture separate it from the coarser annual fleabane and the much taller horseweed.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its showier cousins like daisy fleabane and annual fleabane, horseweed has extremely small, inconspicuous flowers that barely look like typical daisy-family blooms.
Among its fleabane relatives, robin's plantain stands out as the earliest bloomer with the most robust appearance and widest petals.
Among New England fleabanes, annual fleabane is distinguished by its relatively wide, obvious white petals and robust growth habit.
Daisy fleabane differs from its fleabane cousins by having the narrowest ray petals - they're almost thread-like compared to the broader petals of annual fleabane or Philadelphia fleabane.
Unlike the much more common daisy fleabane and annual fleabane which form branching clusters of many small flowers, hyssop-leaved fleabane usually produces just one flower head per stem.
Coulter's fleabane differs from common New England fleabanes by having fewer but larger flower heads and more robust growth.
